vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Mr. D.**

Mr. D. is a 52-year-old married man who presents as a composed, articulate individual, though his posture is rigid and his eyes frequently scan the room during our sessions. He has been a school principal for the past fifteen years in a suburban district, a role he describes as his "calling." The event that reshaped his life occurred fourteen months ago, during what was supposed to be a routine evening.

Mr. D. had stayed late for a parent-teacher conference. As he exited the main building and walked toward his car in the staff parking lot, a man emerged from between two vehicles. He demanded Mr. D.’s wallet and phone. Mr. D. complied immediately, speaking calmly as he often does with upset students. The assailant, apparently enraged by Mr. D.’s composure, struck him twice in the face with a metal object, fracturing his orbital bone and knocking him to the ground. He lay there, bleeding, listening to the man’s footsteps fade, until a janitor leaving the building found him.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. D. returned to work after only ten days, believing that "staying busy" was the best medicine. He now describes that decision as a mistake. He finds himself unable to walk through the parking lot after dark without his heart hammering against his ribs. He has begun arriving at work before dawn, not out of diligence, but because the empty, well-lit building feels safer than the shadowed exterior. He parks directly under the single floodlight nearest the door, a habit he finds embarrassing but cannot break.

His wife, a middle school teacher, has noticed the changes. He no longer tolerates the back porch in the evenings, claiming the neighbor’s motion-sensor light triggers a "crawling sensation" on his skin. He has become irritable with her, snapping when she walks up behind him unexpectedly. At school, his staff describe him as "distant" and "on edge." A veteran teacher recently resigned; Mr. D. realizes he barely registered her goodbye, his mind consumed with scanning the hallways for potential threats.

The most profound change is in his internal world. He describes a constant, low-grade hypervigilance, a feeling of "waiting for the next bad thing." He cannot watch movies with violence, even fictional ones. A car backfiring outside his office window causes him to drop his coffee. He avoids the parking lot entirely now, delegating dismissal duty to his vice principal, a decision that fills him with shame. He feels he has abandoned his post, that he is no longer the steady leader he once was.

He reports nightmares two to three times a week, not of the assault itself, but of variations: being chased through the school’s empty hallways, finding his office door locked from the inside, or seeing the janitor’s face morph into the assailant’s. He wakes drenched in sweat, convinced for several seconds that the attack is happening again.

Mr. D. is a deeply private man. He has told no one at work about the extent of his struggles, believing that a principal must be "unshakeable." He feels a profound sense of disconnection from his own life, as if he is watching himself perform the role of principal from a great distance. He used to love the sound of children’s laughter in the playground; now it feels like a noise he must endure. He says, with a flat, hollow tone, that he feels "like a ghost in my own building." His score on the PCL-5 is 58, indicating severe PTSD symptoms, but for him, the number is less important than the simple, daily reality of feeling unsafe in the one place he was always, unequivocally, in control.
